intro: A quiet F-minor tune keeps returning with more voices around it, until five soft chords stop everything before the coda. Frank Lévy plays Chopin’s Fourth Ballade, his most intricate conversation at the piano.

cues.title: C major opens the door
cues.text: Repeated Gs sound high in the piano over C-major harmony. The melody falls gently, then rests on E. For seven bars, Chopin keeps the Ballade’s F minor waiting outside.
cues.evidence: Chopin, Ballade Op. 52, Joseffy edition, bars 1–7: repeated G octaves, C-major harmony and the held E. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=422
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The F-minor tune
cues.text: The first theme winds through F minor, its melody repeatedly leaning on notes a semitone from their neighbours. A quiet accompaniment rocks beneath it. When the phrase returns, Chopin adds little turns and faster notes inside the same line.
cues.evidence: Joseffy edition, bars 8–36: first theme and its ornamented restatement; C–D♭–B♮–C at the opening of the theme.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Charlotte on the title page
cues.text: Chopin gives the Fourth Ballade to Baroness Charlotte de Rothschild in its dedication. He writes it in 1842, a year after the Third; this is the last of his four works to bear the title.
cues.evidence: Date, dedicatee and place as the last Ballade: Mieczysław Tomaszewski, Fryderyk Chopin Institute. https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/115_ballade-in-f-minor

cues.title: A swaying B♭-major song
cues.text: The second theme sings in B♭ major, piano e dolce — softly and sweetly. The right hand plays a chordal melody above a gently swaying bass. After the first theme’s curling line, these phrases move in broader steps.
cues.evidence: Joseffy edition, bars 80–99; Tomaszewski identifies the B♭-major sicilienne and piano e dolce marking. https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/115_ballade-in-f-minor
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The Three Budrys?
cues.text: In the preface to his edition of the Ballades, the pianist Alfred Cortot tied this one to Mickiewicz’s poem The Three Budrys: three brothers sent off by their father to seek treasure, who come home with three Polish brides. Nothing Chopin wrote confirms it.
cues.evidence: Alfred Cortot’s attribution of the Fourth Ballade to Mickiewicz’s Trzech Budrysów, as reported in the preface to Chopin’s Letters, coll. Henryk Opienski, trans. E. L. Voynich (New York: Knopf, 1931), pp. vii–viii, whose translator adds that she knows of no authentic evidence for any of the Ballade–Mickiewicz links: https://archive.org/details/chopinsletters00chop. Cortot’s own foreword to the Salabert edition was not opened.

cues.title: The opening in A major
cues.text: The introductory melody returns in A major. Its repeated notes and falling phrase are familiar, but the bass has moved from C to A. The piano then unfolds a delicate cadenza, slowing over an A-major chord.
cues.evidence: Joseffy edition, bars 129–134: A-major return of the introduction and cadenza marked dolcissimo and rallentando.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The tune answers itself
cues.text: The first theme returns in D minor, and the left hand answers the right after half a bar. More voices join as the music finds F minor again. The tune now has to sing through its own echoes.
cues.evidence: Joseffy edition, bars 135–145: imitative return beginning A–B♭–D–C♯ in D minor, with the lower voice entering half a bar later; F-minor theme from bar 139.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Ornaments in the high register
cues.text: The first theme comes back as a decorated song, with nocturne-like embellishments floating far up the keyboard above the harmony. Jim Samson calls it a “cantabile-decorative treatment of exquisitely moulded ornamental melody”.
cues.evidence: Jim Samson, Chopin: The Four Ballades (Cambridge University Press, 1992): “a cantabile-decorative treatment of exquisitely moulded ornamental melody” (found by full-text search at the Internet Archive; the page itself was not read). Joseffy edition (Mutopia Project), bars 152–168: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/ftp/ChopinFF/O52/ballade-4/ballade-4-lys/ballade-4.ly
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: D♭ major across the keyboard
cues.text: The second theme returns in D♭ major. The left hand sweeps through arpeggios while the right sings above it in chords. The gentle B♭-major song has become a passage that reaches across the whole piano.
cues.evidence: Joseffy edition, bars 169–191: second-theme return in D♭ major over wide left-hand arpeggios.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Five chords over C
cues.text: After the great rush, five quiet chords sound over a bass C. The upper notes change; the bass stays. The last C-major chord hangs in the air for several bars, then leaves a silence before the coda.
cues.evidence: Joseffy edition, bars 203–210: five chord attacks over C, with the final C-major chord tied across bars 207–210.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The coda breaks loose
cues.text: A low F releases the coda. Semiquaver triplets dart between the hands, with sharp accents and chromatic turns. The soft C-major chord has led straight into the Ballade’s most strenuous F-minor writing.
cues.evidence: Joseffy edition, bars 211 onwards: F bass at the coda’s opening, semiquaver triplets and accented chromatic figuration.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: C major opens onto F minor
transitions.from: Intro · Repeated Gs over C major
transitions.how: The introduction holds E over C-major harmony and a fermata. A C pickup starts the first theme, which curls through F minor at a tempo. The left hand settles into a regular accompaniment beneath the quieter melody.

transitions.title: The hands settle into B♭ major
transitions.how: The first theme’s running notes settle into a B♭-major song, piano e dolce. The right hand sings in chords, with D at the top, while the left hand rocks between bass notes and supporting chords.
transitions.evidence: Joseffy edition, bars 79–85; B♭-major sicilienne and marking also described by Tomaszewski at https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/115_ballade-in-f-minor.

transitions.title: A major recalls the first page
transitions.to: Intro · The opening in A major
transitions.how: The developing passage reaches A major, with A in the bass. The introduction’s repeated-note melody returns above it. Its last phrase slows into a cadenza marked dolcissimo, whose arpeggios spread the A-major chord across both hands.
transitions.evidence: Joseffy edition, bars 128–134: A-major introductory return, dolcissimo cadenza and rallentando.

transitions.title: One hand answers the other
transitions.from: Intro · The opening in A major
transitions.to: A′ · The hands imitate each other
transitions.how: The A-major cadenza ends under a fermata. The right hand starts the first theme in D minor, marked legato; half a bar later, the left hand repeats its opening notes. The answering lines lead back towards F minor.
transitions.evidence: Joseffy edition, bars 134–140: A-major cadenza, D-minor imitation and subsequent F-minor phrase.

transitions.title: D♭ major carries the second song
transitions.from: A′ · The hands imitate each other
transitions.to: B′ · D♭ major over sweeping arpeggios
transitions.how: The first theme’s decorated phrases lead into the second song in D♭ major. The left hand opens out into wide arpeggios, and the right-hand melody rides above them in chords. The gently swaying rhythm survives the much larger accompaniment.
transitions.evidence: Joseffy edition, bars 168–175: D♭-major second-theme return and wide left-hand arpeggios.

transitions.title: The bass stops on C
transitions.from: B′ · D♭ major over sweeping arpeggios
transitions.to: Link · Five quiet chords over C
transitions.how: The rush ends with a C-major chord and a fermata over the rest. Five quiet chords follow. A low C remains beneath their changing upper notes, and the last chord, C major again, is held across several bars.
transitions.evidence: Joseffy edition, bars 201–210: C-major cadence, rest with fermata, and five quiet chords above a C bass.

transitions.title: The held C releases a low F
transitions.from: Link · Five quiet chords over C
transitions.how: The held C-major chord ends in silence. A low F begins the coda, and both hands leap into semiquaver triplets. The dominant harmony has resolved to F minor, but the quiet waiting has become rapid, accented piano writing.
transitions.evidence: Joseffy edition, bars 207–213: held C-major chord, rests, F bass and the coda’s semiquaver triplets.

composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: He brought the opera singer’s breath and the mazurka’s wayward accents to a piano that could whisper across a room.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; composition with Józef Elsner in Warsaw, 1826–29
Warsaw · Paris from 1831 · summers at Nohant
Piano lessons, publishing and occasional concerts
The piano, from a few lines of mazurka to concertos and sonatas
composer.background:
In February 1832, a twenty-one-year-old Polish pianist played in the Pleyel rooms in Paris. Chopin had arrived the previous autumn, with two concertos behind him. The concert caught the attention of the city’s publishers; teaching soon supplied his living. He would spend the rest of his life in a profession that depended on people hearing him at close quarters. The great public virtuosos travelled from triumph to triumph. Chopin stayed in Paris and gave lessons.

He was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810. His father, Nicolas, had come from France and worked as a tutor; his mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska, was Polish. They moved to Warsaw while Fryderyk was still a baby, when Nicolas obtained a teaching post at the Lyceum. At seven the boy already had a polonaise in print. Wojciech Żywny taught him the piano, with Bach and Mozart among his models; Józef Elsner later gave him a rigorous training in composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music.
